extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A Patent Trial and Appeal Board Final Written Decision resolving patentability of challenged claims in an inter partes review, applying standards for claim construction, anticipation, obviousness, level of ordinary skill, and objective indicia of non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art — Envtl. Designs factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors pertinent to a determination of the level of ordinary skill in the art include: “(1) educational level of the inventor; (2) type of problems encountered in the art; (3) prior art solutions to those problems; (4) rapidity with which innovations are made; (5) sophistication of the technology; and (6) educational level of workers active in the field.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all such factors may be present in every case, and one or more of these or other factors may predominate. The Board may adopt a definition reflecting a team of skills where appropriate (e.g., researchers in molecular biology/virology plus protein engineering). Citation: Envtl. Designs, Ltd. v. Union Oil Co., 713 F.2d 693, 696–697 (Fed. Cir. 1983).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; in construing terms we look principally to the intrinsic evidence of record, examining the claim language itself, the written description, and the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same claim construction standard used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b). See Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc); DePuy Spine, Inc. v. Medtronic Sofamor Danek, Inc., 469 F.3d 1005, 1014 (Fed. Cir. 2006); 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to construe claim terms (Nidec/Vivid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only terms 'that are in controversy, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy' need to be explicitly construed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may decline to construe terms not necessary to resolve the proceeding. See Nidec Motor Corp. v. Zhongshan Broad Ocean Motor Co., 868 F.3d 1013, 1017 (Fed. Cir. 2017) (quoting Vivid Techs., Inc. v. Am. Sci. & Eng’g, Inc., 200 F.3d 795, 803 (Fed. Cir. 1999)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specification to supply express definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification may provide an express definition of a claim term, which controls claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification expressly defines a term, the Board will apply that definition (here, the ’248 patent expressly defines 'treat'/'treatment'). Dependents can support constructions (e.g., a dependent claim reciting reduced hemorrhages supports that 'treating' includes partial alleviation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific construction applied: 'treating a coagulopathy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Construed as 'prophylaxis and/or therapy and/or cure of this coagulopathy' which includes partial alleviation of symptoms, for any duration of therapeutic efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied based on the intrinsic evidence and the express definition in the specification (Ex. 1001, 5:19–26) and support from dependent claim 16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in IPR final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner must demonstrate unpatentability of challenged claims by a preponderance of the evidence in the inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory IPR burden applied by the Board in determining patentability in its Final Written Decision under 35 U.S.C. § 318(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard: reasonable likelihood of prevailing
rubrics_metrics.description: At institution, the Board determines whether the information presented in the petition establishes a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail in challenging at least one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reasonable likelihood is shown, the Board may institute an inter partes review as to the challenged claims (referenced here as basis for institution in Paper 15, Decision on Institution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness legal framework (Graham and KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. The question is resolved using underlying factual determinations: (1) scope/content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill; and (4) objective evidence (when available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply an 'expansive and flexible approach' to obviousness; combination that yields only predictable use of prior art elements is likely obvious. See Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1 (1966); KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex, Inc., 550 U.S. 398 (2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness requires motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires more than showing the prior art contains separate references covering each limitation; it requires that a person of ordinary skill would have selected and combined those prior art elements in the normal course of research and development to yield the claimed invention, and have a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Unigene Labs., Inc. v. Apotex, Inc., 655 F.3d 1352, 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2011). Reasonable expectation of success need only be reasonable, not absolute (Pfizer, OSI Pharms distinctions discussed). Hindsight must be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (§102) — prior art disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation requires that a single prior art reference disclose every limitation of the claimed invention (i.e., claim elements are found in the prior art reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If established, a claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 102 (e.g., §102(b) ground based on Stafford was pleaded). The Board may decide anticipation grounds but need not if other grounds dispose the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of non-obviousness and their use
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, industry praise and copying, and unexpected results; such evidence may be the most probative in the record but does not necessarily control the obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective indicia must be considered in context of whether the invention as a whole would have been obvious. They can tip the scales but are weighed with other evidence. See Transocean, Piasecki, Stratoflex references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for objective indicia (ClassCo/Fox Factory/Brown & Williamson)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must establish a nexus between the objective evidence and the merits of the claimed invention; nexus is presumed only when the patentee shows the asserted objective evidence is tied to a specific product that embodies the claimed features and is coextensive with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee bears burden to establish nexus; presumption shifts burden to challenger to rebut. 'Coextensive' means the product is essentially the claimed invention (unclaimed features must be insignificant). Evidence must be reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims. See ClassCo, Fox Factory, Brown & Williamson, Rambus, Campbell Soup, and related Federal Circuit authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coextensiveness / commensurate-in-scope standard
rubrics_metrics.description: For a presumption of nexus, the marketed product must embody the claimed features and be coextensive with them; 'coextensive' means the product is the invention disclosed and claimed and unclaimed features are insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board assesses whether objective indicia evidence is reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims (Fox Factory; Campbell Soup discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and weight of objective indicia evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even strong objective indicia may be insufficient to overcome a strong prima facie showing of obviousness; objective indicia may often be most probative but do not necessarily determine outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board evaluates nexus, commensurateness, and probative weight; examples: industry adoption, praise, or clinical trial activity must be tied to claimed invention to be given substantial weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success standard (OSI Pharms and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill must have had a reasonable expectation of success in combining prior art teachings to achieve the claimed invention; unpredictability in the art does not preclude a finding of obviousness if a reasonable expectation existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation need only be reasonable, not absolute. Distinguish fields where no reliable indicator or mechanism exists (OSI Pharms, Univ. of Strathclyde examples). Evaluate predictability of the field and available indicators of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions in specification as evidence for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions or statements in the patent's specification may be relied upon when assessing whether claims would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may consider specification statements that indicate predictability or expectations of substitutions (citing Koninlijke Philips NV v. Google LLC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims can inform claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim recitation can support a construction of a broader independent claim (e.g., Claim 16's recitation that expression 'reduces and/or prevents hemorrhages' supports that 'treating' includes partial alleviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dependents to interpret scope and meaning where intrinsic evidence supports doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion on addressing instituted grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the petitioner prevails on challenged claims, the Board need not decide other instituted grounds that are unnecessary to resolve the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board has discretion to decline to decide additional instituted grounds once the petitioner has prevailed on all challenged claims (citing SAS Inst. Inc. v. Iancu; Bos. Sci. Scimed, Inc. v. Cook Grp. Inc.; In re Gleave; Beloit Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural note: final written decision and related notices
rubrics_metrics.description: This decision is a Final Written Decision under 35 U.S.C. § 318(a); parties seeking judicial review must comply with notice and service requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 90.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Patent Owner pursues amendment via reissue or reexamination after this Decision, Board reminds Patent Owner of April 2019 Notice Regarding Options for Amendments and continuing obligation to file updated mandatory notices (37 C.F.R. § 42.8(a)(3), (b)(2)).
